entry.evidence: Among these perturbations, the impact of variations in sea level on velocity changes inferred from seismic interferometry of ambient noise is not well known.

sequences.source_document: g22_W4283165407.xml.txt (published text; PDF for figure pages)

steps.action: Posed the question of how sea level variations affect ambient-noise seismic velocity changes, building on Wang et al. (2017) and known ocean loading of the Japanese crust.
steps.quote: It is less well known how changes in sea level, such as its current global sea level rise, affect seismic velocity changes.

steps.action: Stated the expectation that ocean influence on seismic velocity is strongest at the coast and decays with distance inland, and set out to estimate its spatial scale.
steps.quote: The influence of the ocean should be strongest in the coastal environment and should decrease with increasing distance to the ocean.

steps.action: Assembled 2015–2017 records from 99 Hi-net stations (306 pairs) and JMA sea level and atmospheric pressure gauges; computed daily mean sea level, assuming non-tidal processes dominate.
steps.quote: We used seismic data for 99 Hi-net seismic stations in Chugoku and Shikoku

steps.action: Estimated dv/v from the coda of vertical-component noise cross-correlations (0.1–0.9 Hz, 100 s window from d/1 km/s) by stretching, with a sliding 1-year reference and 10-day current stacks.
steps.quote: Seismic velocity changes were estimated with stretching interpolation method

steps.action: Checked the quality of the dv/v estimates by their stretching correlation coefficients (lowest ~0.5; 210 of 306 pairs above 0.6) against values used in published studies.
steps.quote: Most of the station pairs (210 of 306) have stretching correlation coefficients greater than 0.6

steps.action: Named atmospheric pressure loading, correlated with sea level (r up to -0.68), as a rival influence on seismic velocity that loads both inland and coastal regions.
steps.quote: it is necessary to distinguish the imprint of the sea level variations on seismic velocity changes from the influence of atmospheric pressure fluctuations

steps.action: Designed a band search (10 days to 3 years) for periods where station-averaged sea level and pressure are decorrelated (|r| < 0.1, insignificant at alpha = 0.001 by t-test), yielding 12.5–274 days.
steps.quote: We searched for the period bands where the sea level cycle was most weakly correlated with atmospheric pressure.

steps.action: Bandpass-filtered sea level and dv/v, kept pair correlations significant at p < 0.001, grouped pairs into 92 coastal-distance clusters, and averaged absolute correlations; a decreasing trend appeared at 64–274 days.
steps.quote: The resulting scatterplot indicated a trend of decreasing correlations with increasing coastal distance in the time series filtered within the range of 64–274 days

steps.action: Set a linear-regression t-test (alpha = 0.001, n = 92 clusters) of averaged absolute correlation against distance to choose the band, followed by a leave-one-out jackknife.
steps.quote: testing the hypothesis of a linear relationship between the correlation coefficient and distance to the coast

steps.action: Compared the regression across many period bands: R mostly negative and significant for sub-bands near 52–274 days, weaker and not significant when the shortest period is below 52 days.
steps.quote: When the shortest period is smaller than 52 days (e.g., 50- 274 and 41–274 days), the correlation turns weaker

steps.action: Ran the jackknife over the 92 clusters for the 64–274-day band: all replications gave R between -0.4 and -0.45 with p < 0.001.
steps.quote: For this period band, the correlation for all 92 jackknife replications varies within -0.4 to -0.45

steps.action: Selected 64–274 days as the optimum band (R = -0.42, p = 0.000099) and built an interpolated correlation map.
steps.quote: Based on these results, we selected 64–274 days as the optimum period band (Fig. 7a).

steps.action: Mapped pair-level correlations in the chosen band: 126 pairs significantly negative and 62 significantly positive; correlations stronger near the coast.
steps.quote: 126 station pairs had statistically negative correlations

steps.action: Excluded atmospheric pressure: in the same band, pressure versus dv/v shows no distance trend (R = 0.14, p = 0.2).
steps.quote: indicating that the trend in Fig. 7a is unlikely to reflect the perturbation from the atmospheric pressure.

steps.action: Argued against rainfall: annual precipitation shows no clear trend with coastal distance, although its 64–274-day cycle resembles sea level, so an infiltration effect is hard to evaluate.
steps.quote: the decreasing trend in Fig. 7 is not associated with the amount of precipitation.

steps.action: Compared load magnitudes in the band: Earth tide ~170 Pa (from cited tide amplitudes), atmospheric pressure ~800 Pa, sea level ~17 cm or ~1700 Pa; concluded the ocean dominates the forcing.
steps.quote: These comparisons show that the magnitude of the sea-level change is larger than the contribution from atmospheric pressure variations and earth tides.

steps.action: Proposed the mechanism, drawing on cited GPS loading studies (van Dam 1997; Wahr 2013): ocean loading bends the land and dominant vertical stress compresses the subsurface, changing inland stress and dv/v.
steps.quote: seismic velocity changes could be ascribed to inland stress changes due to sea level variation.

steps.action: Offered three untested rival factors for positive versus negative correlations: in situ stress state, dominant crack orientation, and hydraulic conductivity or lithology.
steps.quote: we consider several possible factors that may cause such variations, for example, the in situ stress state, the orientation of cracks, and hydraulic conductivity.

steps.action: Kept the claim that sea level affects coastal dv/v with distance decay, called the study exploratory, and called for a quantitative ocean-mass-redistribution model.
steps.quote: Our results support the hypothesis that seismic velocity changes in coastal regions are affected by variations in sea level.

Estimate the spatial scale of ocean influence through decay with coastal distance
Atmospheric pressure, rainfall, Earth tides; later three rival factors for sign

Jackknife stable; the trend weakens in wider bands and pressure control shows no trend
Kept: distance-decay regularity in the 64–274 day band; mechanism interpretive

end.claim: In the 64–274-day band, the station-cluster-averaged absolute correlation between sea level and seismic velocity change decreases with distance from the coast (R = -0.42, p = 0.000099) over coastal distances of about 0–45 km in Chugoku–Shikoku, 2015–2017.

decisive_move.sentence: Regressing cluster-averaged absolute correlations against coastal distance across many period bands is what produced the significant distance-decay trend, and with it the chosen band.

gates.evidence: Action: the data are archived Hi-net and JMA records; the distance-decay hypothesis shaped the analysis (distance clusters) but not the acquisition (§2 ¶1, §5 ¶2). Claim: the regression t-test at alpha = 0.001 could fail and did fail for many bands (§7 ¶1), and a pressure control was run (§9 ¶1). However, the reported band was chosen because it maximized |R| among many tested bands, with no stated correction for multiple comparisons (§7 ¶2). Registration: thresholds (alpha = 0.001, |r| < 0.1) are justified in the text, but nothing is stated as fixed before the data were seen; the band was selected post hoc (§4 ¶3–¶4, §7 ¶2).

novelty_claims.quote: Among these perturbations, the impact of variations in sea level on velocity changes inferred from seismic interferometry of ambient noise is not well known.
We show that consideration of station’s distance from the coast helps to distinguish the influence of sea level on seismic velocity monitoring.

limits:
Headline claim: regularity_in_range (distance decay in the 64–274-day band).

Sub-claims at lower status:
- The imprint reaches 'at least dozens of kilometers' inland: regularity_in_range, bounded by the ~45 km station range.
- Ocean loading causes vertical compression and inland stress change: best_explanation at most. It rests on cited GPS loading studies and a load-magnitude comparison, not a test.
- Crack orientation, in situ stress and lithology or permeability explain the signs: status none. These are untested possibilities, and the authors call the work exploratory (§11 ¶5).

What the document does not show:
- The search over period bands is a large garden of forking paths: the band was picked by maximal |R| among many tested bands (Table S1), with no correction for multiple testing (inference).
- Station pairs share stations, so the 92 distance clusters are not independent samples (inference).
- Only pair correlations with p < 0.001 entered the clusters, a selection step whose effect is not reported.
- Absolute values merge the 126 negative and 62 positive pairs, so the regularity is in correlation magnitude, not sign.
- The rainfall rival is only partly excluded: its cycle resembles sea level in this band, and the paper says an infiltration effect is hard to evaluate (§9 ¶2).
- No quantitative loading model is compared with the data.
- No replication in another region or period, and no alternative dv/v method.
- No review file was supplied, so no review sequence is coded.

A minor inconsistency: the abstract gives 0.0036–0.0155 cycle/day for 64–274 days. No explicit disagreement with published work is stated; Wang et al. (2017) is built on, not disputed.
